catalog_locator: Section 2.4 STRESS, printed p. 413 (pdf p. 434 of the ANU Open Research PDF; the whole section sits on p. 413, 2.5 PHONOTACTICS opens p. 414); re-opened during this reading as and checked against the page image (running head '2.3 Vowels 413').
catalog_quote: The position of stress within a word is perhaps the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology. We have the following source material: [a] Walker marks each vowel with either ¯ or ˘; these marks apparently indicate accent rather than quantity (see the comment in Roth 1899, p.1 of Appendix). [b] Norman uses the same marks, probably in the same way. [c] Milligan says 'when a double consonant or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent, as in the English words cunningly, peppery, cobbler, pipkin.' This somewhat elusive statement perhaps means that the vowel preceding a sequence of two consonants (in Milligan's orthography) bears stress. [d] Tindale's transcriptions. [e] The Fanny Cochrane Smith recordings. [f] The 1972 Crowley recordings of Mrs. Heffernan and Mrs. Mundy. From these sources it appears that a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, whereas a trisyllabic word can be stressed on either first or second syllable. Our only general conclusion concerning stress in Tasmanian is thus: any syllable except the last can bear stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Tasmanian languages as a whole (no variety-specific statement exists): disyllables carry stress on the first syllable; trisyllables on the first or the second; the final syllable is never stressed. The authors decline to fix a single position beyond 'non-final'. Taylor 2006 (MA thesis) reads the same 19th-century diacritics as showing regular stress on the first word element, i.e. initial stress, and rejects C&D's formulation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Crowley & Dixon say nothing. Taylor 2006: 160 says the non-initial elements show 'either no stressing.. or at best secondary stressing'; p. 259 mentions secondary stressing of following word elements and not infrequently of final elements.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllabic words vary between first- and second-syllable stress; Milligan's 1859 remark (vowel before a written double consonant / cluster carries the accent) is reported as a possible conditioning factor but called 'elusive'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, inferred philologically from isolated citation forms: 19th-century recorders' macron/breve diacritics (Walker 1832-34 at Flinders Island, Norman, the Robinsons), Milligan's orthographic remark, Tindale's 1930s phonetic transcriptions, c.1900 wax-cylinder songs of Fanny Cochrane Smith, and Crowley's 1972 recordings of two rememberers whose pronunciation was 'almost wholly assimilated to that of Australian English'. No living speakers; no phrase-level information. The statement covers all Tasmanian varieties jointly, not Ben Lomond/Cape Portland specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is NOT specific to benl1235: Crowley & Dixon 1981 treat the whole Tasmanian corpus ('Tasmanian', all 15 vocabulary regions) as one phonological reconstruction and give a single stress conclusion for all of it. Within that chapter (pp. 402-403) 'Piper River, Cape Portland and Ben Lomond form an interrelated group.. could be dialects of a single language', which is the unit Glottolog calls benl1235 and ISO 639-3 CR 2019-047 calls 'Northeastern Tasmanian / Pyemmairrener (T7, T9, T14) [benl1235] (Ben Lomond, Cape Portland-Piper River)'. The stress evidence C&D list (Walker's and Norman's diacritics, Milligan's remark, Tindale, the c.1900 Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders, Crowley's 1972 recordings of Mrs Heffernan and Mrs Mundy) is drawn from mixed or south-eastern-dominated material; the 1972 words happen to match Piper River / Cape Portland forms (p. 405-406) but C&D do not localise their stress conclusion. G.W. Walker (1898: 152-153) reports that the catechist at Wybalenna translated Genesis into 'the language of the Ben Lomond tribe', but his own marked vocabulary (pp. 169-170) is not attributed to a tribe. Sibling check dirs tasm1247 (family bookkeeping code) and neta1235 (North Midlands) rest on the same page; a catalog entry for benl1235 would be a family-level inheritance, not a variety-specific description.

sources.note: Pan-Tasmanian: stress position 'the most elusive aspect'; from Walker/Norman diacritics, Milligan's remark, Tindale, the Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders and the 1972 Crowley recordings, disyllables are always initial-stressed, trisyllables stressed on 1st or 2nd; 'any syllable except the last can bear stress'. Also p. 397: from the c.1900 F.C. Smith recordings 'the only inferences that can be drawn concern the placement of stress'. Groups Piper River, Cape Portland, Ben Lomond as one interrelated NE group (p. 402-403).
